title: VB0-00614
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the "principal/male claimant"), XXXX XXXX (the "associated/female claimant"), XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "minor claimant/their son"), and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "minor claimant/their daughter"), citizens of Turkey, claim refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act" or "IRPA").1 Allegations

The claimants are Alevis from Turkey. The female claimant's father was arrested and beaten by police in XXXX 2007, resulting in his death on XXXX XXXX, 2007. The doctor could not report the torture because he didn't want to lose his job. Two of the female claimant's sisters escaped due to persecution. The male claimant was also repeatedly taken into custody and beaten and tortured by police. This happened about six times, the last times being XXXX 2009 and XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, both of which occurred when the claimants were coming out of church. Fundamentalists also insulted the male claimant hundreds of times and beat him approximately eight times in 2008 and 2009, usually when coming from church. The children were also insulted and slapped at school because of their Alevi faith. The family left their home in XXXX, Turkey, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, travelling via the United States, and came to Canada on XXXX XXXX 2010. The family claimed refugee protection in Edmonton two days later. Determination
I find that the claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. Analysis
The claimants' identities as citizens of Turkey are established by their testimony and the supporting documentation filed, namely their passports and their birth certificates.2

The onus is on the claimants to submit sufficient, credible and trustworthy evidence to the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) in order to establish that they have a well-founded fear of persecution.3 I find that the claimants did not do so. Their testimony included inconsistencies and omissions. They were vague in describing their regular religious practices as Alevis or what it was that led to their being targeted on that basis. I find that the claimants did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that their evidence regarding alleged persecution against them is credible.

The male claimant stated that he had been subject to numerous incidents of assault and mistreatment from police and from Muslim extremists due to his Alevi religion. However, his testimony about these alleged incidents included serious inconsistencies. When I asked the claimant about the most recent incident of police mistreatment he could recall, he said it was when he was taken to the police station on XXXX XXXX, 2007, which he said was in connection with legal and medical documents he presented in evidence.4 This would have been almost three years before he left Turkey on XXXX XXXX, 2010. His Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative, however, outlines two specific incidents of being arrested, beaten and detained by police within the year just before the claimants left their country, one in XXXX 2009, and one on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009. The claimant made no mention of these alleged incidents in response to my question about recent incidents, even when I repeated my question about whether there had been any further problems with police after the alleged XXXX 2007 incident.

When I pointed out the incidents referred to in the PIF narrative, the claimant seemed unsure about what I was talking about, and when I asked why he did not describe these alleged incidents of police mistreatment in the months prior to leaving Turkey, he said he did not know but that he could have been absent-minded. When his counsel again asked him why he did not mention these two arrests, he said he was focussing more on the medical report, and that he must have been distracted by that. Later, when the female claimant was testifying, she added her explanation for the inconsistency that her husband was nervous in the hearing and that perhaps he did not want to mention certain matters in front of their children. I do not accept these explanations. The husband could have told me or his lawyer if he had wanted to provide some testimony with his children absent from the hearing room. Meanwhile, I do not find that nervousness can account for such a serious omission of the two most recent alleged incidents, which included not only arrests but also alleged beatings and overnight detentions.

In addition, the wife's testimony about these alleged incidents was also inconsistent from the PIF. Although the PIF states that in both the 2009 incidents the police arrested, detained and beat up the male claimant, the female claimant stated in oral testimony that in one of these incidents he was arrested and in the other he was only beaten up but not arrested. When asked about this inconsistency she noted that she had said there were up to six incidents that occurred in 2008 and 2009, but that she only mentioned two of them by date. This does not address the question of the inconsistent evidence about whether the claimant was arrested in the most recent alleged attacks, and is not a satisfactory explanation.

Meanwhile, with respect to the alleged XXXX XXXX, 2007 arrest, even though the claimant had some documents he said related to this incident, he was not clear in explaining how the medical and police reports corroborated his testimony, and the documents themselves are not explicit in describing alleged injuries resulting from an alleged beating by police. The claimant was also vague in his testimony about this incident, which is not mentioned at all in the PIF. He could not at first remember which year it occurred, and he had trouble describing what he was actually doing in the XXXX XXXX XXXX which would have led to his being arrested. Although he said there was a trial, he could not recall how long after the alleged arrest the trial had occurred.

Counsel submitted that the claimants' difficulties in recollecting some of the events that happened to them were due to the fact that the claimants had suffered so many incidents throughout their lives, and that the female claimant had said that she had tried to forget about the past, which-he noted-was not uncommon for victims to do as a way of healing. However, in this case the claimants knew that they were preparing for a refugee hearing, and had prepared and affirmed their PIF narrative prior to the hearing. The allegations that the male claimant was arrested and detained on several occasions are foundational to establishing the past persecution they said they endured. Although explanations about forgetting or avoidance might address problems remembering minor details about their allegations, I do not accept that the claimants would not be able to recall even major aspects of the most recent incidents that they said occurred. These alleged incidents are key to their claim, and I find that the inconsistencies and vague testimony are indicative of a lack of credibility.

In addition, aside from alleged police mistreatment, the PIF also alleges enduring hundreds of insults from fundamentalists in Turkey, as well as three beatings by fundamentalists in 2008 and five beatings in 2009. The husband did not mention these alleged beatings either when I asked him about recent incidents of mistreatment. Furthermore, although in oral testimony the parents and children testified about specific allegations of mistreatment of the children in school, such as the daughter allegedly being put in a garbage can, and the son getting a scar on his neck from a nail, these particular incidents were not mentioned in the PIF. The claimants did not present medical reports from these alleged injuries, or police reports from the times they said they reported alleged assaults on their children. They stated that the doctors and police refused to give them copies of the reports, but they did not present any evidence demonstrating efforts to secure these documents.

The claimants stated that most of the mistreatment was directed against them when they were on their way to weekly attendance at the religious services at the cem house. However, they were vague in describing specific Alevi practices and what happened at the services. For example, when I asked the male claimant what the differences were between Sunni Muslims and Alevis, he said it was that Muslims attended mosques and Alevis attended cem houses. He described music but did not describe other unique religious practices that are referred to in country documentation.5 In the same way, the female claimant mentioned teaching about twelve imams, but when I asked about other differences noted in the documentation, she could not spontaneously describe Alevi practices until I highlighted the information in country material. Counsel noted the female claimant's explanation that she did not want to talk about things before the Member questioned her. This is not satisfactory. I made it clear to the claimants that I wanted them to describe aspects of their practice that would help me to ascertain if they actually did regularly attend the weekly services as they alleged. However, their answers to questions did not establish a level of knowledge that would be reasonably expected from faithful attendees at the cem house services.

Furthermore, when I asked the male claimant if anyone in his family changed their attendance at the cem house services as a result of the mistreatment they received when they tried to go to services, he said there had been no changes. However, the PIF states that because the wife was afraid for her safety she did not attend church as often as her husband. When I pointed this out to the male claimant, he asked me if she had said that this happened, then said he did not remember that it was in the PIF but that it could be true. There was no explanation for his failure to remember his wife's alleged change in worship service attendance as a result of alleged fear of mistreatment.

The claimants' testimony included inconsistencies and omissions with respect to key allegations. Their testimony about the regular practice of their religion, which they said led to the persecution against them, was vague. They provided documentation about some court proceedings and medical treatment with respect to an alleged incident that had been omitted from the PIF, but the documentation does not make clear reference to the persecution they described. At the same time, they failed to provide other medical or police documents about other incidents that they did refer to in their narrative or in their oral testimony. Although they have membership cards for an Alevi association, they did not demonstrate the kind of knowledge about regular religious practices that would be reasonably expected for people who attended had services weekly for most of their lives. I find that the claimants did not present sufficient reliable and credible evidence to establish that they face a serious possibility of persecution in Turkey based on their Alevi religion.

Counsel referred in his submissions to the fact that the female claimant's sister and her family had had a successful refugee claim in Canada in June 2010.6 He submitted that their acceptance as refugees was highly persuasive, and that there should be consistencies in the decisions from the Refugee Protection Division when the claimants are from the same religious faith and the country conditions they faced are the same. However, as noted by counsel, a decision of another Board member is not binding on me. In addition, the claimants did not submit a copy of the family members' PIF or other materials outlining the basis of the claim, which also-according to the claimants-included an aspect of forced military service, which is not a factor in the claim before me. I therefore do not know the specifics of the basis for the sister's family's positive determination, and I do not find that there is sufficient information for me to conclude that this family is similarly situated.

Having found the claimants to lack credibility with regard to the primary allegations central to their claim, including in particular the most severe allegations of beatings and police detentions of the male claimant, I have considered whether there is any residual evidence to support a claim for refugee protection. As noted by counsel, country documentation notes that Alevis were unable to state their religion on their national identity card, and that "there were reports of societal abuses and discrimination based on religious affiliation, belief, and practice."7 However, this document also notes that "Alevis freely practiced their beliefs and built cem houses (places of gathering)," and that the government "generally respected religious freedom."8 Other documents do note that Alevis faced discrimination in employment and societal viewpoints,9 but that their situation "has improved in recent years."10 I find that the documentary evidence is not sufficient in itself to establish that discriminatory treatment experienced by Alevis would constitute persecution, either on an individual or a cumulative basis. There is no additional evidence advanced in support of the claim to be persons in need of protection pursuant to section 97 of the Act that is different from that advanced in support of the claim to be Convention refugees pursuant to section 96 of the Act. Therefore, in this case, having found the factual foundation of the claim of severe mistreatment to lack credibility, I do not find that there is other evidence that would provide a well-founded fear of persecution or a foundation for establishing a personal risk to life, or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or danger of torture for the claimants pursuant to s. 96 or s. 97 of the Act.

For the foregoing reasons, I conclude that XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX are not Convention refugees and not persons in need of protection and I therefore reject their claims.
